name: Resonance tuning (formant)

lead: Resonance tuning means adjusting the shape of the throat and mouth so vocal tract resonances, called formants, shift and give the voice a different timbre. Voice-modification communities use it aiming for a deeper, darker or more masculine sound.

Formants are broad peaks in the sound spectrum created by acoustic resonance in the vocal tract, and changes in mouth and lip shape move them; for example, lip rounding lowers them. Vowels are identified mostly by the first two formants. The acoustics is well established, though no studies test deliberate tuning for perceived attractiveness.

paras: People practise with spectrogram or formant-display apps, changing tongue, lip and throat position while recording and comparing the sound. It is typically combined with pitch and breath work over weeks.
No risks are documented in the sources reviewed. As with any vocal practice, pain or hoarseness is a sign to stop.

web.title: Europe PMC: formant dispersion and attractiveness studies

angle.text: Reshaping the vocal tract moves its resonances, or formants, to give the voice a deeper, darker timbre. Formant acoustics is well established science; its use as a deliberate voice-improvement method has not been tested.

lead: Resonance tuning is the deliberate shaping of the throat, mouth and lips so that the voice's formants, the broad spectral peaks created by acoustic resonance in the vocal tract, move to different frequencies. People use it to change how their voice sounds, for example to make it come across as deeper, warmer, brighter or more projected, without changing the pitch set by the vocal folds.[1][2]

Voice is part of the impression a person makes, and formants are among the acoustic features listeners use to judge a speaker. Studies of vocal attractiveness have found that low, closely spaced formants tend to accompany larger, older and higher-testosterone male speakers, and that women rated voices with low formant dispersion as more attractive in some samples, which is why formant adjustment appears in discussions of making a voice sound fuller or more masculine.[3] In voice therapy for transgender clients, resonance and pitch are described as the traits with the greatest effect on perceived gender, and clinicians teach lip, tongue and larynx adjustments to move resonance up or down.[4][5]

The acoustics is well described: vowels are mostly identified by the first two formants, lip rounding lowers formants, a longer tract lowers resonance frequencies, and trained singers add a peak near 3000 Hz called the singer's formant, or ring.[1][6][7] Controlled studies of resonance tuning as an appearance practice were not found; the available research covers formant acoustics, listener perception, voice therapy and actor and singer training.[4][8][3]

paras: A formant is defined as the broad spectral maximum produced by an acoustic resonance of the vocal tract. Ludimar Hermann proposed the concept in 1894 and coined the term while addressing how vowels stay recognisable across speakers with different vocal tract lengths.[1]

The first formant is higher for open vowels such as /a/ and lower for closed ones such as /i/ and /u/, and the second is higher for front vowels and lower for back vowels; lip rounding lowers both. Wikipedia lists average male values of about 240 Hz and 2400 Hz for F1 and F2 of /i/, against about 850 Hz and 1610 Hz for /a/.[1] Changes in vocal tract length scale all resonance frequencies.[1]

Vocal resonance in general is described as enhancement of the voice's basic sound by the air-filled spaces it passes through, changing timbre or intensity. The pharynx is described as the most important resonator because of its position, size and adjustability, while the tongue, jaw and lips reshape the oral cavity and act as a final filter. These supraglottal structures are under voluntary control, whereas the larynx is not directly consciously controlled.[2]

Voice teachers describe a range of colours from dark, chest-based resonance to bright, head and nasal resonance. Chest resonance is said to add warmth and depth, nasal resonance brightness and projection, and mouth resonance a conversational colour.[2]

Formants arise because the vocal tract is a tube whose shape selectively amplifies certain frequencies of the sound produced by the vocal folds. Moving the lips, tongue, jaw, soft palate or larynx changes the shape and length of the tube and so moves the formants without changing the pitch set by the folds.[1][2]

The singer's formant, also called squillo, ring or ping, is a cluster of resonance in roughly the 2 to 5 kHz range that Wikipedia says is believed to result from a narrowing of the aryepiglottic fold just above the larynx. It allows a voice to be heard over an orchestra, and singers cited for it include Maria Callas, Luciano Pavarotti and Birgit Nilsson.[7] Too much of it is described as shrill and too little as defeating its purpose, and it can give an aged voice an impression of youth.[7] Trained male singers show a clear peak around 3000 Hz that is absent in ordinary speech.[1][6]

sections.h: Formants, body size and attractiveness research
paras: Formants have been studied as cues to body size and sex. A 2016 review notes that humans can voluntarily modulate fundamental and formant frequencies, the features linked to impressions of body size and sex, so speakers can shift the impressions their voice conveys.[9]

Studies indexed in Europe PMC describe the listener side. In a 2006 study, Bruckert and colleagues had 102 women rate recordings from 26 men; men with low-frequency formants and small formant dispersion tended to be older, taller and to have higher testosterone, and listeners used formant components to estimate age though not height accurately.[3] A 2010 study of natural speech from a dating game by Hodges-Simeon, Gaulin and Puts found that low mean pitch, low formant dispersion and high intensity predicted women's attractiveness ratings, with low formant dispersion rated attractive only by women in the fertile cycle phase.[3]

Puts, Apicella and Cardenas (2012) reported in US and Hadza forager samples that a measure called formant position was more sexually dimorphic and more strongly related to height than formant dispersion, and in the US sample it predicted upper-body strength.[3] A 2008 study of 40 men found higher salivary testosterone associated with lower fundamental frequency, but the link with formant dispersion was limited and not significant.[3]

Other work looks at wider impressions: McAleer, Todorov and Belin (2014) had 320 participants rate 64 brief utterances of 'hello' and found ratings fit a two-dimensional space of valence and dominance, with attractiveness of male voices rising with both; Babel and colleagues (2014) found attractiveness was predicted by a combination of acoustic features including cues to apparent talker size and conformity to community speech norms.[3] Klofstad and colleagues (2012) found that men and women preferred lower-pitched versions of both male and female leaders.[3]

In voice therapy for transgender people, vocal tract length is used to explain perceived pitch: a male vocal tract is described as 10 to 20 percent longer than a female one, giving lower resonance. Clients are taught lip retraction to shorten the tract, or larynx lowering and chest resonance to deepen the sound, and semi-occluded exercises such as phonating through a straw.[4]

Wikipedia's overview of voice feminization and masculinization states that fundamental frequency and voice resonance have the greatest effect on perceived femininity, that formant changes can alter perceived gender even when pitch stays the same, and that lip protrusion and retraction are used to lengthen or shorten the tract.[5] For masculinization it lists controlling larynx height, breath support, relaxation and chest resonance, and notes that testosterone usually deepens the voice but not always to the desired level.[5] Surgical options exist for pitch, mostly for transgender women, and are usually considered after therapy.[5]
Clients who complete voice therapy report high satisfaction. A 2012 review cited there rated the evidence base as weak, with most studies at the lowest level of the evidence hierarchy.[4][5]

sections.h: Use in actors, singers and speakers
paras: A 2022 study in the Journal of Voice followed 11 student actors through 16 months of Linklater Voice training and measured acoustic and perceptual changes, including formant frequencies F1 to F4. It reported a significantly larger perceived pitch range, a trend toward more balanced phonation and a trend toward a darker perceived voice quality.[8]

Singers use the same mechanics to add ring and carry, and speakers use chest or head resonance to colour how they sound.[2][6][7] Voice coaches and speech-language pathologists teach these adjustments in clinical and performance settings.[4]

Resonance tuning is the acoustic principle behind advice about making a voice sound deeper, warmer or brighter: a darker timbre is associated with a longer effective tract or more chest resonance, and a brighter one with lip retraction or forward placement.[2][4] Because listeners link low formants with larger body size and rate them as more attractive in some studies, people interested in how their voice comes across are interested in this lever alongside pitch.[9][3] Practitioners describe changes in lip, jaw and larynx position as the means, and results are judged by ear or recorded acoustic analysis.

No studies found testing resonance tuning specifically as an appearance or attractiveness practice. Related research includes the 16-month Linklater training study in 11 actors, speech-language pathology work on resonance for transgender clients whose evidence base a cited review rated as weak, and listener-perception studies of formants and attractiveness with samples ranging from 26 to 320 people.[4][8][3]

lore.intro: Resonance is discussed in voice-improvement circles mostly as the way to make a voice sound deeper or more authoritative without changing pitch; community material on the practice was limited, so the claims below are drawn from the acoustics and voice-therapy literature.

claims.claim: Changing mouth and throat shape can make the voice sound deeper without lowering pitch
A voice with low formants sounds more attractive
Formants reveal a speaker's size and strength
Resonance training noticeably changes how listeners read a voice's gender or character
The singer's formant gives a voice ring and makes it carry
